title: The Impact of Mandatory Corporate Social Responsibility Reporting on Liquidity and Risk
text: This study investigates whether mandatory corporate social responsibility (CSR) reporting ameliorates liquidity and reduces risk for stocks. Moreover, we explore whether these impacts vary with regulated company category and stakeholder influence capacity. For a mandatory CSR reporting regulation in Taiwan, we assess the policy’s effects using difference-in-differences (DID) modeling. The results show that mandatory CSR reporting significantly increases liquidity and reduces idiosyncratic risks. However, the effect on systematic risk is asymmetric—a high (low) systematic risk is accompanied by a positive (negative) market return; namely, a large (small) price increase (decrease) caused by a positive (negative) market return. This aligns with the insurance-like benefits argument. These findings suggest investors hold on to CSR firms because of increased information transparency and good financial performance during a recession. The improved liquidity is more significant for firms in the electronics and chemical industries and for firms with a large equity share owned by domestic institutional investors. Idiosyncratic risk is reduced more for the latter two. The findings provide feedback on mandatory CSR reporting to policy makers and provide reference for firms and investors.

title: Common Ownership Network and the Expansion of Female Board Representation
text:
Abstract
This study investigates the potential of common ownership to expand the pool of female director candidates and alleviate the underrepresentation of women on corporate boards. Using the California Senate Bill No. 826 and peer female director appointments as quasi-experimental settings, our findings demonstrate that firms under common ownership exhibit greater female board representation and a higher propensity to appoint new female directors. Furthermore, these firms show an increased likelihood of women attaining leadership positions on board committees. Our results remain robust to accounting for the activeness of the Big Three, underscore the network effect of common ownership on the supply side of the labor market for female directors.

title: Socially Responsible Investing: A Financial Trend with a Conscience
text:
In today’s global economy, investors are increasingly concerned not only with financial returns but also with the ethical implications of their investments. Socially Responsible Investing (SRI) has emerged as a prominent strategy that combines financial considerations with social and environmental values. This approach empowers investors to align their portfolios with their beliefs and has reshaped the investment landscape.

What is Socially Responsible Investing (SRI)?
SRI considers both financial returns and social/environmental impacts. It involves evaluating investments based on ethical, social, and environmental criteria, often referred to as Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors. By excluding or favoring certain sectors or companies, SRI seeks to promote responsible business practices and contribute to sustainable development. Larry Fink, CEO of BlackRock, emphasizes this dual focus: “We focus on sustainability not because we’re environmentalists, but because we are capitalists and fiduciaries to our clients.”


The Historical Context
The roots of SRI can be traced back to the religious movements of the 18th century, where certain investments were avoided on moral grounds. The modern SRI movement gained traction during the 1960s, focusing on issues like apartheid, labor rights, and environmental protection. Today, SRI has evolved into a comprehensive investment philosophy that incorporates various ethical considerations.


Methods of SRI

Screening: Investors may exclude or include companies based on specific ESG criteria. Negative screening avoids sectors such as tobacco and weapons, while positive screening favors companies with strong social and environmental performance.
Shareholder Advocacy: Through engagement and proxy voting, investors can influence corporate behavior and promote responsible governance.
Impact Investing: Targeting investments that generate both financial returns and positive social or environmental impacts, impact investing seeks to create tangible societal benefits.
Community Investing: By investing in community development projects, investors can support underserved areas and foster local economic growth.



Relevance to Corporate Finance and Governance
SRI has significant implications for corporate finance and governance. It highlights the interconnectedness of financial performance and societal well-being, challenging traditional investment models. Corporations are encouraged to improve their ESG performance to attract SRI capital, driving a broader shift towards transparency, accountability, and long-term sustainability.


Conclusion
Socially Responsible Investing represents a transformative approach that aligns financial objectives with ethical values. By integrating social and environmental considerations into investment decisions, SRI offers a holistic perspective that resonates with a growing number of investors. It reflects a profound shift in the investment world, one that acknowledges that profitability and responsibility need not be mutually exclusive.
Whether you are an individual investor or a financial institution, understanding and implementing SRI can offer a meaningful way to align your investment strategy with your values. As this field continues to evolve, it promises to play a critical role in shaping a more sustainable and conscientious financial future.

title: Common Ownership Network and Board Gender Diversity
text: This study examines the network hypothesis, proposing that interconnections among top executives facilitated by common institutional ownership contribute to greater board gender diversity. The effect is particularly pronounced in firms with higher female representation among industry peers. Using California Senate Bill No. 826 and peer female director appointments as quasi-experimental settings, empirical evidence shows that firms under common ownership are more likely to increase female board representation, appoint new female directors, and facilitate interlocking female directorates across portfolio firms. Furthermore, these firms exhibit a higher propensity for women to attain leadership positions on board committees, reinforcing the role of ownership networks in expanding opportunities for female directors beyond mere representation. The findings remain robust after accounting for the influence of the Big Three, highlighting the importance of common ownership as a structural mechanism that shapes governance practices, facilitates director mobility, and influences the broader labor market for female executives.

Data Preparation
Next, we will prepare the data by calculating daily returns for both the stock and the market index. tq_transmute() is used to manipulate stock data by creating a new variable, stock_return. Stock (or market) returns are calculated as the difference between the current and the past return divided by the past return. Because we are looking at daily data, the past return refers to the return that occurred on the previous trading day. na.omit() is used to drop observations with missing values.

  tq_transmute(select = adjusted, 
               mutate_fun = periodReturn,

               mutate_fun = periodReturn,

title: Estimating Beta Coefficients
text:
Systematic Risk
The beta coefficient is the slope of the regression line. We can extract it from the regression model.

# Extract the beta coefficient
beta_coefficient <- tidy(model) %>%
  filter(term == "market_return") %>%
  select(estimate) %>%
  pull()

cat("The estimated beta coefficient for", 
    stock_ticker, "is", 
    round(beta_coefficient, 2))

The estimated beta coefficient for AAPL is 1.2


The estimated beta coefficient tells us how sensitive the stock’s return is to the market’s return. For instance, if the beta is 1.2, it means that if the market return increases by 1%, the stock’s return is expected to increase by 1.2%, indicating higher volatility relative to the market.

title: Estimating Beta Coefficients
text:
Idiosyncratic Risk
Idiosyncratic (unsystematic) volatility represents the portion of the stock’s volatility that is not explained by market movements. It can be estimated by taking the standard deviation of the residuals from the market model. The residuals (\(\epsilon\)) represent the differences between the observed stock returns and the returns predicted by the market model.

# Calculate the residuals from the market model
residuals <- resid(model)

# Calculate the standard deviation of the residuals
idiosyncratic_volatility <- sd(residuals)

cat("The estimated idiosyncratic risk for", 
    stock_ticker, "is", 
    round(idiosyncratic_volatility, 2))

The estimated idiosyncratic risk for AAPL is 0.01

title: Estimating Beta Coefficients
text:
Footnotes


There is no unique answer to how to set the estimation window. In this case, we choose to look at the previous three years of daily returns. You can choose any time horizon that suits your analysis. This is based on the implicit assumption that the estimated beta using historical data represents the stock’s riskiness in recent periods.↩︎
You might be wondering why the risk-free rate is ignored in the market model. Indeed, some people would regress \(R_i-R_f\) on \(R_M-R_f\), where the risk-free rate, \(R_f\), is typically measured by Treasury Bill yields. Including the risk-free rate will make beta coefficient slightly different, but the change will be usually minor. For simplicity, you may choose to ignore the risk-free rate.↩︎

Cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) are the sum of abnormal returns over a specified event window. We need to define an event date and the event window around this date.

# Define the event date and the event window

  filter(date >= event_date - event_window & 
           date <= event_date + event_window)

The pipe operator allows you to pass the output of one function directly into another function, making your code cleaner and easier to read.

1. Fetching Stock Data
We use R to create an equally weighted portfolio consisting of four stocks: ExxonMobil (XOM), Walmart (WMT), NVIDIA (NVDA), and Apple (AAPL). Using tidyquant to fetch stock prices via Yahoo Finance. Note that the corresponding ticker for a given stock can be found on its website.

library(tidyquant)
library(tidyverse)
library(highcharter)
library(DT)


# Define stock tickers and date range
stocks <- c("XOM", "WMT", "NVDA", "AAPL")
start_date <- "2023-01-01"
end_date <- "2023-04-30"
# Download stock prices
prices <- tq_get(stocks, from = start_date, to = end_date)
# Print out interactive table
datatable(prices) |> 
  formatRound(columns = c("open","high","low","close","adjusted"), digits = 2)

title: R Note 2 - Portfolio Formation
R Note 2 - Portfolio Formation
text:
3. Portfolio Valuation and Return Calculation

3.1 Portfolio Value
Calculate the portfolio value for each trading day:

portfolio <- prices |> 
  inner_join(initial_positions, by = "symbol") |> 
  mutate(position_value = shares * adjusted) |> 
  group_by(date) |> 
  summarize(total_value = sum(position_value)) |> 
  arrange(date)

datatable(portfolio) |> 
  formatRound(columns = c("total_value"), digits = 2)







3.2 Portfolio Returns

A. Calculating returns from the net value of portfolio
Returns in finance can be calculated using either discrete or continuous methods. Both approaches measure investment performance but have different interpretations and applications. Here presents the key difference between these two:








Feature
Discrete Returns
Continuous Returns




Formula




\[R_t=P_t/P_{t-1}-1\]




\[R_t=ln(P_t/P_{t-1})\]




Interpretation
Simple percentage change
Log-based compounding change


Time Additivity
❌ No
✅ Yes


Compounding
Not considered
Naturally accounts for compounding


Use Case
Short-term analysis (daily, weekly returns), industry
Long-term modeling (portfolio returns, Black-Scholes model), academics



Calculate discrete and continuous returns for the portfolio:

portfolio <- portfolio |> 
  mutate(discrete_return = 100*(total_value / lag(total_value) - 1),
         continuous_return = 100*log(total_value / lag(total_value)))

datatable(portfolio) |> 
  formatRound(columns = c("total_value","discrete_return","continuous_return"), digits = 2)







B. Calculating returns directly from portfolio securities
Similar to the previous method, we calculate discrete and continuous returns for the portfolio through portfoflio stocks directly rather than net value:

individual_ret <- prices |> 
  mutate(
    # 1. assign portfolio weights on corresponding stocks
    portfolio_weight = case_when(
      symbol == "XOM" ~ 0.25, 
      symbol == "WMT" ~ 0.25, 
      symbol == "NVDA" ~ 0.25, 
      symbol == "AAPL" ~ 0.25
    ),
    # 2. individual returns (grouped by each stock)
    discrete_return = 100*(adjusted / lag(adjusted) - 1),
    continuous_return = 100*log(adjusted / lag(adjusted)),
    .by = symbol
  ) |> 
  select(symbol, date, portfolio_weight, discrete_return, continuous_return) |> 
  # the first obervation of each stock will naturally be missing since there is no lagged value, then we drop it out
  drop_na(continuous_return)
# print out individual returns
datatable(individual_ret) |> 
  formatRound(columns = c("discrete_return","continuous_return"), digits = 2)




# Aggregate returns of four individual stocks by each day (DATE)
portfolio_ret <- individual_ret |> 
  group_by(date) |> 
  summarise(port_return = sum(portfolio_weight*continuous_return),
            .groups = "drop")
datatable(portfolio_ret) |> 
  formatRound(columns = c("port_return"), digits = 4)








3.3 Portfolio Volatility
Calculate variance and volatility (standard deviation) of portfolio returns from individual stocks.
The portfolio volatility (standard deviation of portfolio returns) is given by:
\[ \sigma_p = \sqrt{ w^T \mathbf{\Sigma}w}\]
Where:

\(\sigma_p\) = Portfolio volatility
\(w\) = Column vector of asset weights (\(w_1, w_2, w_3, w_4\))
\(\mathbf{\Sigma}\) = Covariance matrix of asset returns
\(w^T\) = Transposed weight vector


# sigma for each stock
portfolio_volatility <- individual_ret |> 
  group_by(symbol) |> 
  summarise(sigma = sd(continuous_return),
            .groups = "drop")
datatable(portfolio_volatility) |> 
  formatRound(columns = c("sigma"), digits = 4)




# stock weights
weights <- c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25)
# individual stock volatilities (standard deviations)
volatilities <- portfolio_volatility$sigma
# correlation matrix
returns_wide <- individual_ret |> 
  select(symbol, date, continuous_return) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = symbol, values_from = continuous_return)
# Calculate correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(returns_wide[, -1], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
datatable(cor_matrix) |> 
  formatRound(columns = 1:4, digits = 4)




# Compute covariance matrix
cov_matrix <- (volatilities %*% t(volatilities)) * cor_matrix
# Calculate portfolio volatility
portfolio_volatility <- sqrt(t(weights) %*% cov_matrix %*% weights)
# Print result
cat(sprintf("Portfolio return is %.2f percent", portfolio_volatility))

Portfolio return is 1.21 percent

title: Greenwashing and Its Impact on Corporate Operating Performance
text: Some firms may engage in greenwashing to cultivate a sustainable image, creating a discrepancy between actual practices and disclosed information. Using a sample of publicly listed firms in Taiwan from 2019 to 2023, this study categorizes ESG-related actions into symbolic and substantive dimensions to construct a firm-level greenwashing measure, further decomposed into two dimensions: the exaggeration score, which captures the extent to which symbolic actions exceed substantive actions, and the silence score, which reflects underreporting of symbolic actions relative to substantive performance. Empirical findings present a significant negative association between greenwashing and operating performance. These results validate the applicability of the greenwashing measure proposed in this study, and suggesting that both substantive improvements in governance and a restrained, consistent approach to sustainability disclosure contribute meaningfully to better operating performance.

In this document, we will estimate the beta coefficient of a stock. The beta coefficient measures the systematic risk of a stock relative to the overall market. We will download stock prices and market index prices using the tidyquant package, compute the returns, and then perform a regression analysis.



Following the previous note, we collect stock price data of NVIDIA using package tidyquant. First, we need to install and load the required packages. Ensure you have tidyquant, dplyr installed.

# Load required packages
library(tidyquant) 
library(dplyr)
library(broom)
library(DT)
library(ggplot2)

We will download stock prices for a chosen stock (e.g., NVIDIA Inc., ticker: NVDA) and a market index (e.g., S&P 500, ticker: ^GSPC) from Yahoo Finance during the estimation window 2020-2022.1 You can find any corresponding tickers that you would like to explore from its website.

The market model is a statistical model that describes the relationship between the returns of a stock and the returns of the overall market.2 It is a simple linear regression model that can be expressed as follows:
\[R_i=\alpha+ \beta \times R_m + \epsilon\]
where:

\(R_i\) is the return of the individual stock.
\(\alpha\) (alpha) is the intercept, representing the stock’s return independent of the market’s return.
\(\beta\) (beta) is the slope coefficient, representing the sensitivity of the stock’s return to the market’s return (this is the beta coefficient we are estimating).
\(R_m\) is the return of the market.
\(\epsilon\) (epsilon) is the error term, representing the part of the stock’s return not explained by the market return.

In this section, we will perform a linear regression of the stock returns on the market returns to estimate the beta coefficient. The beta coefficient indicates how much the stock’s return is expected to change in response to a 1% change in the market’s return. A beta greater than 1 indicates that the stock is more volatile than the market, while a beta less than 1 indicates that the stock is less volatile. Theoretically, beta coefficient is considered as a measure of systematic risk of a stock.

# Perform the linear regression
model <- lm(stock_return ~ market_return, data = returns_data)

# Display the summary of the regression model
summary(model)

The beta coefficient is the slope of the regression line. We can extract it from the regression model.

  filter(term == "market_return") |> 
  select(estimate) |> 
  pull()

    stock_ticker, "is",

The estimated beta coefficient tells us how sensitive the stock’s return is to the market’s return. For instance, if the beta is 1.66, it means that if the market return increases by 1%, the stock’s return is expected to increase by 1.66%, indicating higher volatility relative to the market.



Idiosyncratic (unsystematic) volatility represents the portion of the stock’s volatility that is not explained by market movements. It can be estimated by taking the standard deviation of the residuals from the market model. The residuals (\(\epsilon\)) represent the differences between the observed stock returns and the returns predicted by the market model.

# Calculate the residuals from the market model

# Calculate the standard deviation of the residuals

    stock_ticker, "is", 
    round(idiosyncratic_volatility, 2))

We also estimated the idiosyncratic volatility by calculating the standard deviation of the residuals from the market model. The beta coefficient helps us understand the stock’s systematic risk in relation to the overall market, while idiosyncratic volatility measures the stock-specific risk not explained by market movements.

text:
Alternative Strategy Designs and Student Exercise

💡 Suggested Extensions

RSI with MA filter: only act on RSI signals when the price is above MA200 (trending up). This avoids buying into a falling knife.
MACD: the MACD() function in TTR computes the Moving Average Convergence/Divergence oscillator, which generates its own crossover signals.
Stochastic Oscillator: stoch() in TTR. Similar logic to RSI but tracks where a closing price sits relative to its recent high-low range.
DCA with a Boost: stick to NT$20,000/month normally, but invest NT$40,000 whenever RSI < 30 (doubling down when the market is oversold).
Value Averaging: a variant of DCA where the target portfolio value grows by a fixed amount each month; you invest more when the market falls and less (or even sell) when it rises too fast.

title: When Black Swan Meets Green Swan: ESG Engagement and Financial Resilience in U.S. Airlines during COVID-19
text: It is a challenge for firms to survive the combination of black and green swans, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. With the airline industry as our target laboratory, we investigate the commitment to ESG of firms and its effects during this black-swan period. We find that airline companies who have implemented sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) experienced better operating performance during the pandemic. Companies with greater financial pressure are found to allocate less resources to ESG when passenger numbers plummet. Overall, the worsening financial situation resulting from the black swan does not significantly decrease the attention given to green swan initiatives.

title: Sustainable Fund Ownership to Corporate Financial Performance
text: This study investigates the impact of sustainable fund holdings on portfolio firms’ sustainability performance and financial performance, and further examines the mediating role of sustainability performance in this relationship. The empirical results show that when sustainable funds increase their holdings in a company, not only does the firm’s sustainability performance improve significantly, but its financial performance also benefits. Further analysis reveals a positive correlation between a firm’s sustainability performance and financial performance, and that once sustainability performance is taken into account, the direct impact of sustainable fund holdings on financial performance weakens, supporting the mediating effect of sustainability performance. Overall, sustainable funds can exercise a monitoring function by encouraging portfolio firms to enhance their sustainability efforts, thereby improving long-term financial outcomes. Based on these findings, this study suggests that the regulatory agencies continue to focus on the establishment and operation of sustainable funds, reinforcing fund managers’ role in overseeing firms’ sustainability development, so as to further promote the growth and maturity of sustainable finance in Taiwan.

title: Selective Ties: Common Ownership and the Restructuring of Board Interlocks
text: We examine how common institutional ownership influences the formation of board interlocks. Competing views suggest that common owners may expand or selectively restructure governance networks to enhance monitoring. Using the staggered financial institution mergers during 2001–2010 as our identification strategy, we find that an increase in common ownership reduces overall board interlocks, largely driven by a decline in cross-industry interlocks; however, within-industry interlocks remain largely unaffected by the level of common ownership. The aforementioned effect is stronger in firms with weaker governance and greater managerial ability. Overall, our findings support a focused monitoring perspective, indicating that institutional investors selectively reshape board networks rather than broadly expand them.

title: Spillover Effects of Common Ownership in M&As
text: This project investigates whether common institutional ownership generates spillover effects on firms not directly involved in merger and acquisition (M&A) transactions. Existing studies primarily focus on outcomes for acquiring and target firms, leaving the broader market implications of M&A activity underexplored. This project shifts attention to peer firms connected through shared institutional owners and examines how changes in common ownership affect their strategic behavior and governance responses around M&A events. To address endogeneity concerns, the project exploits financial institution mergers as plausibly exogenous shocks to common ownership. This project contributes to the literature on common ownership and corporate strategy by documenting an indirect channel through which institutional investors may shape firm behavior and market competition.

title: The Impact of Mandatory Corporate Social Responsibility Reporting on Liquidity and Risk
text: This study investigates whether mandatory corporate social responsibility (CSR) reporting ameliorates liquidity and reduces risk for stocks. Moreover, we explore whether these impacts vary with regulated company category and stakeholder influence capacity. For a mandatory CSR reporting regulation in Taiwan, we assess the policy’s effects using difference-in-differences (DID) modeling. The results show that mandatory CSR reporting significantly increases liquidity and reduces idiosyncratic risks. However, the effect on systematic risk is asymmetric—a high (low) systematic risk is accompanied by a positive (negative) market return; namely, a large (small) price increase (decrease) caused by a positive (negative) market return. This aligns with the insurance-like benefits argument. These findings suggest investors hold on to CSR firms because of increased information transparency and good financial performance during a recession. The improved liquidity is more significant for firms in the electronics and chemical industries and for firms with a large equity share owned by domestic institutional investors. Idiosyncratic risk is reduced more for the latter two. The findings provide feedback on mandatory CSR reporting to policy makers and provide reference for firms and investors.

text:
Abstract
Using trade-level data from the Taiwan Stock Exchange, we document an asymmetric pattern of liquidity provision by individual investors who serve as de facto market makers. Specifically, on average, individual investors provide more liquidity during market declines. We further investigate the impact of asymmetric individual liquidity provision on market efficiency. Despite being uninformed, individual investors’ liquidity provision ameliorates market efficiency more during market declines. Our results suggest that individual investors provide liquidity to help those with private information correct prices toward efficient prices, in turn, enhancing market efficiency.

title: R Note 5 - Behavioral Finance and Lottery-Like Stock Strategies
text:
Introduction
In Note 4, we explored a moving-average crossover strategy and benchmarked it against a buy-and-hold position on 0050.TW. Those strategies rest on technical analysis — the idea that past price patterns convey information about future prices. In this note, we step beyond pure technicals and explore behavioral finance-motivated strategies that exploit systematic biases in investor preferences.
The behavioral finance literature documents that many investors — particularly retail investors — exhibit a preference for stocks with lottery-like payoffs: assets offering a small probability of a large positive return, even at the cost of a low or negative expected return. This preference distorts prices in predictable ways and gives rise to cross-sectional return anomalies that academic researchers and quantitative traders have studied extensively.
Three lines of empirical work guide this note:

Bali et al. (2011) propose the maximum daily return over the previous month (MAX) as a proxy for lottery-like features and document that high-MAX stocks subsequently underperform by more than 1% per month in U.S. data.
Lin and Liu (2018) show that this MAX–return relation is concentrated among stocks preferred by individual investors, with the spread effectively zero among institutionally-held large-caps.
Kumar et al. (2024) broaden this evidence by combining several skewness proxies — MAXRET, lottery index (LIDX), jackpot probability (JACKPOT), and expected idiosyncratic skewness (ESKEW) — and showing that skewness sentiment amplifies a wide range of cross-sectional anomalies, primarily through the underperformance of overpriced (short-leg) stocks.

The pedagogical aim of this note is fourfold:

Introduce a cross-sectional portfolio sorting framework using a basket of Taiwan 50 (0050.TW) constituents.
Implement a MAX-based long-short strategy following Bali et al. (2011).
Implement a lottery index (LIDX) strategy combining price, volatility, and skewness, following Kumar et al. (2016) and Kumar et al. (2024).
Implement an idiosyncratic-volatility (IVOL) strategy, drawing on the seminal puzzle of Ang et al. (2006) — but using Note 3’s simpler market-model residuals to keep the implementation tractable.


Note on scope: The original studies use thousands of U.S. stocks across decades. With a small Taiwanese basket and a short window, our portfolio sorts are illustrative rather than statistically definitive. The goal is to learn the methodology, not to make causal claims about Taiwanese market efficiency.

title: R Note 5 - Behavioral Finance and Lottery-Like Stock Strategies
text:
1. Theoretical Background

1.1 Why Should Lottery-Like Stocks Underperform?
Classical asset pricing (CAPM) predicts that only systematic risk (covariance with the market) is priced. Idiosyncratic skewness and extreme tail outcomes should not matter, because rational investors hold well-diversified portfolios and diversify these features away.
Behavioral models depart from this view in two complementary ways:

Cumulative Prospect Theory (Barberis and Huang 2008): Investors overweight small probabilities of large gains, leading them to overpay for positively-skewed (lottery-like) assets. In equilibrium, these assets earn lower expected returns.
Optimal Beliefs / Skewness Preference (Brunnermeier et al. 2007; Mitton and Vorkink 2007): When investors are under-diversified, idiosyncratic skewness enters their utility directly. They willingly hold positively-skewed stocks at a discount to expected return.

Both frameworks predict the empirical pattern documented by Bali et al. (2011): stocks with extreme positive recent returns earn lower subsequent returns.


1.2 The Role of Individual Investors
Lin and Liu (2018) argue that this anomaly should concentrate among stocks where individual investors are most active, because retail investors are the natural carriers of the behavioral biases above. Institutional investors are typically well-diversified and treat lottery-like holdings as informed bets rather than skewness preference (Kumar and Page 2014).


1.3 Skewness Sentiment as a Common Mispricing Driver
Kumar et al. (2024) extend this view by showing that skewness preference is not just a single-anomaly phenomenon — it is a common driver of cross-sectional mispricing across at least 11 distinct anomaly strategies. Their evidence works through two channels:

Multiple skewness proxies tell the same story. They compare four skewness measures — MAXRET, LIDX, JACKPOT (the out-of-sample probability of a stock generating a log return \(> 100\%\) in the next 12 months), and ESKEW (expected idiosyncratic skewness from a predictive regression according to Boyer et al. (2010)) — and find that all four interact significantly with mispricing. A one-standard-deviation increase in skewness adds 30%–60% to the predictive power of the combined mispricing measure.
The amplification is short-leg-driven. Skewness has essentially no effect on the long leg (underpriced stocks). The interaction comes entirely from skewness-loving investors bidding up the short leg.

We will not implement JACKPOT or ESKEW directly — both require either a fitted logit panel or a cross-sectional predictive regression that is beyond the scope of a single note. But we will implement LIDX, which is conceptually closely related and computationally tractable, and we will discuss JACKPOT and ESKEW as natural extensions.


1.4 The Idiosyncratic Volatility Puzzle
Ang et al. (2006) document a separate but related puzzle: stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility, measured as the residual standard deviation from a Fama-French three-factor model fit to daily returns within the previous month, earn lower future returns. This contradicts standard intuition that volatility should be compensated, and it has spawned a large literature.
The connection to MAX/skewness is empirically tight. Bali et al. (2011) show that controlling for MAX reverses the IVOL puzzle, and Kumar et al. (2024) conclude that IVOL and skewness exacerbate anomalies for different reasons (IVOL deters arbitrageurs; skewness attracts speculators), but that both effects are present.

A practical simplification. The Ang et al. (2006) IVOL measure uses the daily Fama-French three-factor regression, which requires importing the FF factors and estimating a regression separately for every stock-month. To keep the implementation light, we use the simpler market-model residual standard deviation introduced in Note 3 (regressing the stock on a single market index). This is not identical to Ang et al.’s measure, but it captures the same economic intuition — the part of return volatility unrelated to systematic market movement — and is sufficient for pedagogical purposes. Students interested in the original measure should consult Ang et al. (2006) directly.

section: 8. Caveats and Connections to the Literature
text:
8. Caveats and Connections to the Literature
Several caveats are worth emphasizing to students:

Sample size and power. With ~20 stocks and ~28 months, our terciles contain about 7 stocks each. Bali et al. (2011) use thousands of stocks and four decades; Kumar et al. (2024) use the full CRSP universe from 1963–2015. Any “anomaly” in our small sample is best treated as a teaching artifact, not evidence about the Taiwanese market.
Conditioning matters. Lin and Liu (2018) show that even in the U.S., the MAX anomaly is concentrated in stocks dominated by individual investors. Our basket of Taiwan 50 large-caps is heavily institutionally held, so we might expect the MAX/LIDX/IVOL strategies to underperform here — itself a Lin-and-Liu-style empirical prediction.
Risk adjustment. Production-quality tests adjust returns using factor models (Fama-French 3/5, Carhart momentum). The four-factor and six-factor alphas in Bali et al. (2011) Table III and Kumar et al. (2024) Table 4 are the relevant magnitudes for academic claims. We omit factor adjustment here for clarity.
Transaction costs and short-selling. Our long-short strategies implicitly assume costless short-selling. In Taiwan, shorting individual stocks involves locate costs, securities-borrowing constraints, and tick-rules. Both Bali et al. (2011) and Kumar et al. (2024) emphasize that short-selling frictions help explain why these anomalies persist.
IVOL measurement. Our IVOL is the residual standard deviation from a single-factor market-model regression on daily returns within each month — much simpler than the daily Fama-French three-factor specification of Ang et al. (2006). The two are highly correlated, but a publishable replication would use the original specification.

title: R Note 5 - Behavioral Finance and Lottery-Like Stock Strategies
text:
9. Suggested Extensions

Implement JACKPOT (Conrad et al. 2014): Estimate a logit/probit model predicting whether a stock generates a log return above some threshold (e.g., 50% over 6 months in a Taiwanese context) using lagged firm characteristics, and use the fitted probability as a sort variable.
Implement ESKEW (Boyer et al. 2010): Run a monthly cross-sectional predictive regression of realized skewness on lagged firm characteristics, then sort on the fitted (expected) skewness.
Replicate BCW’s IVOL/MAX horse-race (Bali et al. 2011 Table 9): Double-sort on MAX and IVOL to test whether MAX subsumes the IVOL puzzle. This is the most influential single result in BCW, and replicating it locally is informative.
Extend to MIN as a sanity check. Bali et al. (2011) report that minimum daily return generates the opposite sign — consistent with prospect-theory loss aversion. This provides a useful internal validity check.
Combine into a composite mispricing index. Following Kumar et al. (2024), form a single MIS-style index by averaging decile ranks across MAX, LIDX, and IVOL, and sort on the composite.

text:
10. Student Exercise
Design and implement your own behavioral-finance strategy for a Taiwanese stock universe. Specifically:

Choose a behavioral signal beyond MAX, LIDX, or IVOL (suggestions: 52-week high proximity, total skewness over a 6/12-month window, turnover-based proxies for retail attention, short-interest ratios).
Form portfolios by sorting on your signal each month using terciles or quintiles.
Benchmark against the three strategies in this note plus the equal-weighted buy-and-hold and the TAIEX index.
Discuss whether the results support or contradict the Lin and Liu (2018) prediction that lottery anomalies should be weak in institutionally-held large-caps.

A successful answer demonstrates (a) careful construction of the cross-sectional signal, (b) honest acknowledgment of small-sample limitations, and (c) thoughtful interpretation in light of the conditioning argument in Lin and Liu (2018) and Kumar et al. (2024).

title: When the Watchdog Leaves, the Empire Shrinks: Local Media Closures and Corporate Investment
text: Contrary to the conventional view that weaker external monitoring emboldens self-interested managers, we find that CEOs reduce empire building after a local newspaper closes near firm headquarters. Using a difference-in-differences design exploiting local newspaper closures in the United States from 2003 to 2018, affected firms overinvest less, undertake fewer and smaller acquisitions, and initiate fewer large and diversifying bids. The reduction is most pronounced in cash-financed acquisitions and in transaction categories most closely associated with managerial expansion incentives, while divestiture activity is unchanged. The evidence supports a reputation-preservation channel, in which heightened informational opacity raises financing frictions and managerial career concerns, inducing investment conservatism rather than entrenchment. Our results identify the local press primarily as a producer of information for capital providers rather than as a disciplinarian of managerial slack.

title: Corporate social performance, retail investor trading, and stock price crash risk
text: We investigate the relationship between corporate social performance (CSP) and stock price crash risk in Taiwan, a market dominated by retail investors. While prior literature primarily focuses on environmental performance and institutional monitoring channels, relatively little is known about whether and how investors, particularly retail investors, respond to firms’ social engagement. We find that higher CSP is associated with lower crash risk, and that this relation is stronger among firms with greater retail trading intensity. The results are robust to alternative specifications, including a two-stage Heckman selection model, a dynamic system GMM estimator, and alternative measures. These findings suggest that in retail-dominated markets, CSP affects downside risk through investor behavior, consistent with an attention- and reputation-based channel. Overall, our study highlights that the asset pricing implications of CSP depend on investor composition and are more pronounced when retail participation is high.

title: Week 5: Risk, Beta, and the Market Model
text:
A stock’s total volatility \(\sigma_i\) has two ingredients:

Systematic risk: co-moves with the market. Cannot be diversified away.
Idiosyncratic risk: stock-specific. Vanishes in a well-diversified portfolio.

The market model is the simplest tool to separate the two. And it gives us a single number that captures systematic risk: \(\beta\).

title: Week 5: Risk, Beta, and the Market Model
text:
A stock’s total volatility \(\sigma_i\) has two ingredients:

Systematic risk: co-moves with the market. Cannot be diversified away.
Idiosyncratic risk: stock-specific. Vanishes in a well-diversified portfolio.

The market model is the simplest tool to separate the two. And it gives us a single number that captures systematic risk: \(\beta\).

title: Week 5: Risk, Beta, and the Market Model
section: A linear regression of stock on market
text:
A linear regression of stock on market






NoteMarket model



\[R_{i,t} = \alpha_i + \beta_i\, R_{m,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t}\]



\(R_{i,t}\): stock \(i\)’s return on day \(t\).
\(R_{m,t}\): the market’s return on day \(t\).
\(\alpha_i\): intercept — average performance unrelated to the market.
\(\beta_i\): slope — the sensitivity of the stock to the market.
\(\varepsilon_{i,t}\): residual — the part the market cannot explain.

In R, this is a one-line call to lm().

title: Week 5: Risk, Beta, and the Market Model
text:
What does \(\beta\) mean?
\[\beta_i = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(R_i,\,R_m)}{\mathrm{Var}(R_m)}\]

\(\beta > 1\): stock amplifies market moves — more cyclical.
\(\beta = 1\): stock moves with the market on average.
\(0 < \beta < 1\): stock moves with the market but less than 1-for-1 — defensive.
\(\beta < 0\): stock moves against the market — rare; gold and some hedges.

For tech stocks like NVDA we typically see \(\beta > 1\); for utilities and consumer staples, \(\beta < 1\).

title: Week 5: Risk, Beta, and the Market Model

The data

stock_ticker  <- "NVDA"
market_ticker <- "^GSPC"   # S&P 500

end_date      <- "2026-01-01"

stock_data  <- tq_get(stock_ticker,  from = start_date, to = end_date)

Computing daily returns

stock_returns <- stock_data |>
  tq_transmute(select     = adjusted,

title: Week 5: Risk, Beta, and the Market Model
text:
What the regression can’t explain
The residuals \(\hat\varepsilon_{i,t} = R_{i,t} - \hat{\alpha} - \hat\beta\, R_{m,t}\) are the stock-specific portion of returns.






NoteIdiosyncratic volatility



\[\sigma_{\varepsilon,i} = \mathrm{sd}\!\left(\hat\varepsilon_{i,t}\right)\]



residuals_i <- resid(model)
idio_vol    <- sd(residuals_i)
cat("Idiosyncratic volatility:",
    round(idio_vol, 4), "\n")

Idiosyncratic volatility: 0.0238

title: Week 5: Risk, Beta, and the Market Model
text:
Decomposition of variance
In population:
\[\underbrace{\sigma_i^2}_{\text{total}}
\;=\;
\underbrace{\beta_i^2\, \sigma_m^2}_{\text{systematic}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sigma_{\varepsilon,i}^2}_{\text{idiosyncratic}}.\]

sigma_total <- sd(returns$stock_return)
sigma_mkt   <- sd(returns$market_return)
sys_part    <- beta_hat^2 * sigma_mkt^2
idio_part   <- idio_vol^2

c(total_var = sigma_total^2,
  systematic = sys_part,
  idiosyncratic = idio_part)

    total_var    systematic idiosyncratic 
 0.0011217331  0.0005529311  0.0005688020 


systematic + idiosyncratic should approximately equal total_var — the analysis-of-variance identity behind the market model.

title: Week 5: Risk, Beta, and the Market Model
text:
\(\beta\) is what the CAPM prices
The Capital Asset Pricing Model (Sharpe, 1964) says expected excess return depends only on \(\beta\):






NoteCAPM



\[E[R_i] - R_f = \beta_i \,\bigl(E[R_m] - R_f\bigr)\]



High-\(\beta\) stocks should earn higher expected returns.
Idiosyncratic risk should not be priced — you can diversify it away.

The empirical evidence is mixed (the “low-beta anomaly”), but \(\beta\) remains the single most-cited measure of a stock’s market risk.

title: Week 5: Risk, Beta, and the Market Model
text:
Course connections
What we built this week will be the foundation for two later ideas you’ll meet if you continue:

Cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) in event studies. The market model predicts a stock’s “normal” return; whatever the stock does above and beyond that prediction around an event date is the abnormal return.
Multi-factor models (Fama-French, Carhart). We replace the single market return with several factor portfolios. The R syntax barely changes: lm(R_i ~ MKT + SMB + HML).

title: Week 5: Risk, Beta, and the Market Model

Decomposed total risk into systematic and idiosyncratic parts.

Connected \(\beta\) to the CAPM and to multi-factor extensions.

What is a moving average?
A rolling mean of the last \(n\) days of adjusted close.






NoteSimple moving average



\[MA_n(t) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} P_{t-i}\]

NoteSignal definition

text:
What this kind of comparison teaches
Three serious lessons emerge from looking at the chart honestly:

The MA crossover often lags sharp trend reversals — it buys late and sells late.
A long stretch of sideways prices generates many false signals (“whipsaws”), each costing implicit slippage.
Buy-and-hold, the most boring strategy on the planet, is competitive with — sometimes better than — an active rule.

This is the standard result for naive technical strategies in academic backtests. It is a feature of the problem, not a bug in your code.

title: Week 6: A Working Trading Strategy in R
text:
What we ignored

Transaction costs and slippage: every trade costs money in reality.
Bid-ask spreads: you don’t actually trade at the close.
Survivorship bias: 0050 is the post-2003 winner index.
Look-ahead bias: we used lag() correctly — always check this.
Risk adjustment: we compared raw returns, not Sharpe ratios. A volatile winner is not the same kind of “good” as a smooth winner.

A serious research replication would address every one of these.

Volatility-scaled positions: larger position when realized volatility is low; smaller when high.
Mean reversion: use Bollinger Bands or RSI to fade extremes instead of follow trends.
Calendar rotation: invest only Nov–Apr; cash the rest.

text:
You bought a stock at NT$100. It’s now NT$110.
How much did you make?
Two equally valid answers:

In money: NT$10.
In percentage: 10%.

This week is about percentage returns — and the fact that there are two different definitions, both correct, both used in practice.

title: Week 3: Calculating Returns
text:
Definition






NoteDiscrete return



\[R_t = \frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}} - 1 = \frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}}\]


The intuitive percentage change. If \(P_{t-1} = 100\) and \(P_t = 110\), then \(R_t = 10\%\).
This is the version you see in newspapers, brokerage statements, and industry research.

title: Week 3: Calculating Returns
section: Computing it in R with dplyr

title: Week 3: Calculating Returns
text:
Definition






NoteContinuous (log) return



\[r_t = \ln\!\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}\right) = \ln P_t - \ln P_{t-1}\]


The log return is the instantaneous-growth-rate version of return — the counterpart of continuous compounding from Week 2.
For small changes, \(r_t \approx R_t\). They diverge for large moves.

title: Week 3: Calculating Returns
section: Discrete vs. continuous — side by side
text:
Discrete vs. continuous — side by side

apple <- apple |>
  mutate(R_disc = adjusted / lag(adjusted) - 1,
         r_log  = log(adjusted / lag(adjusted)))

For a typical daily move of \(\pm 1\%\), the two are nearly identical. For a \(+50\%\) jump, \(R = 0.50\) but \(r = \ln(1.5) = 0.405\).

title: Week 3: Calculating Returns
text:
When to use which?









Discrete \(R\)
Continuous \(r\)




Interpretation
Simple % change
Log-based, continuous


Time-additive?
No
Yes


Cross-section sum
Yes (portfolio)
No


Where used
Industry, reporting
Academic research, modelling



The time-additivity of log returns is what makes them the standard in econometrics: a 2-day log return is just the sum of two daily log returns.

title: Week 3: Calculating Returns
text:
Why log returns are time-additive
Over \(n\) days: \[\frac{P_T}{P_0} = \prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\ln\!\frac{P_T}{P_0} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} r_t.\] So \(r_{0 \to T} = r_1 + r_2 + \cdots + r_T\). Sum them.
But the same formula in discrete form is: \[1 + R_{0 \to T} = \prod_{t=1}^{T} (1 + R_t).\] So \(R_{0 \to T} \ne R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_T\). Compound them.

title: Week 3: Calculating Returns
text:
Why discrete returns are cross-section-additive
For a portfolio with weights \(w_i\) summing to 1:
\[R_p = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\,R_i \qquad \text{(exactly)}\] This is exact for discrete returns, and only approximate for log returns.
Practical rule of thumb:

Aggregating across stocks at one point in time \(\to\) discrete.
Aggregating across time for one stock \(\to\) continuous.

title: Week 3: Calculating Returns
text:
Cumulative discrete return
\[R_{\text{cum}} = \prod_{t=1}^{T}(1 + R_t) - 1\]

apple <- apple |>
  mutate(cum_R = cumprod(1 + coalesce(R_disc, 0)) - 1)

cumprod() does the running product; coalesce(R_disc, 0) replaces the first NA with 0 so the cumulative product starts from 1.

title: Week 3: Calculating Returns
text:
Cumulative log return
\[r_{\text{cum}} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} r_t\]

apple <- apple |>
  mutate(cum_r = cumsum(coalesce(r_log, 0)))

Just cumsum() — nothing more.
To convert back to a discrete cumulative return: \(R_{\text{cum}} = e^{r_{\text{cum}}} - 1\).

title: Week 3: Calculating Returns
section: A passive strategy in one line
text:
A passive strategy in one line
The simplest possible “strategy”: buy on day 0, never trade. The return over any horizon is just the price ratio:
\[R_{\text{BH}} = \frac{P_T}{P_0} - 1\]

apple |>
  summarise(BH_return = last(adjusted) / first(adjusted) - 1)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  BH_return
      <dbl>
1      1.21


It sounds trivial — but as we’ll see in Week 6, a well-chosen buy-and-hold often beats more complex active strategies. Don’t dismiss it.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Suppose someone offers you a choice:

Option A: NT$1,000 today.
Option B: NT$1,000 one year from today.

Which is better? Most people pick A. Why?



Suppose someone offers you a choice:

Option A: NT$1,000 today.
Option B: NT$1,000 one year from today.

Which is better? Most people pick A. Why?
Three reasons:

You could invest A and earn interest.
Inflation may erode B’s purchasing power.
B is uncertain — you might not actually get it.




If you can invest at an annual rate \(r\), then NT$1 today grows to NT$(1+r) in one year.
Equivalently, NT$1 next year is worth only NT$\(\frac{1}{1+r}\) today.
This single idea — the discount factor \(\frac{1}{1+r}\) — is the foundation of every valuation formula in finance, from a savings account to a billion-dollar acquisition.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Future Value
Investing \(PV\) today at rate \(r\) for \(n\) years:






NoteFuture value (annual compounding)



\[FV = PV \cdot (1+r)^n\]



PV <- 1000
r  <- 0.05
n  <- 10
FV <- PV * (1 + r)^n
FV

[1] 1628.895


NT$1,000 today becomes NT$1,628.89 in ten years at 5%.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Present Value
Running the relation backwards:






NotePresent value



\[PV = \frac{FV}{(1+r)^n}\]



FV <- 1000
r  <- 0.05
n  <- 10
PV <- FV / (1 + r)^n
PV

[1] 613.9133


NT$1,000 promised in ten years is worth only NT$613.91 today.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Writing a reusable function
Hard-coding numbers is fragile. Wrap the formula in a function:

pv <- function(FV, r, n) FV / (1 + r)^n
fv <- function(PV, r, n) PV * (1 + r)^n

pv(FV = 1000, r = 0.05, n = 10)

[1] 613.9133

fv(PV = 1000, r = 0.05, n = 10)

[1] 1628.895


Now any calculation in the course can call pv() or fv().

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Compounding \(m\) times per year
If interest is paid \(m\) times per year, each period the rate is \(r/m\):






Note



\[FV = PV \cdot \left(1 + \frac{r}{m}\right)^{m\,n}\]



PV <- 1000; r <- 0.05; n <- 10
m <- c(1, 2, 4, 12, 365)
FV_m <- PV * (1 + r/m)^(m*n)
data.frame(periods_per_year = m, FV = round(FV_m, 2))

  periods_per_year      FV
1                1 1628.89
2                2 1638.62
3                4 1643.62
4               12 1647.01
5              365 1648.66


More frequent compounding \(\Rightarrow\) larger FV, but the gains shrink fast.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Continuous compounding
Take \(m \to \infty\):






NoteContinuous compounding



\[FV = PV \cdot e^{r n}, \qquad PV = FV \cdot e^{-r n}\]



PV <- 1000; r <- 0.05; n <- 10
FV_cont <- PV * exp(r * n)
FV_cont

[1] 1648.721


This is the form you’ll meet again in option pricing (Black-Scholes uses continuous compounding throughout).

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
What is an annuity?
An annuity is a stream of equal cash flows \(C\) paid at the end of each period for \(n\) periods. Examples:

Monthly mortgage payments.
Yearly retirement-fund withdrawals.
Coupon payments on a bond.

The present value of all those payments is the sum of \(n\) discounted cash flows.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
The annuity formula






NotePresent value of an ordinary annuity



\[PV = C \cdot \frac{1 - (1+r)^{-n}}{r}\]



annuity_pv <- function(C, r, n) {
  C * (1 - (1 + r)^(-n)) / r
}
annuity_pv(C = 50000, r = 0.04, n = 20)

[1] 679516.3


NT$50,000 every year for 20 years at 4% has a present value of about NT$679,500 — much less than \(20 \times 50{,}000 = 1{,}000{,}000\).

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Perpetuity
Let \(n \to \infty\) in the annuity formula:






NotePerpetuity



\[PV = \frac{C}{r}\]



perp_pv <- function(C, r) C / r
perp_pv(C = 50000, r = 0.04)

[1] 1250000


A NT$50,000 perpetual payment at 4% is worth NT$1,250,000 today — the same logic underlies the Gordon growth model for valuing stocks.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Mixed cash flows: NPV
Most real projects produce unequal cash flows at different times. Sum them all, discounted to today:






NoteNet present value



\[NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t}\]


Decision rule: invest if \(NPV > 0\).

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
NPV in R

cf <- c(-100000, 30000, 35000, 40000, 45000)
r  <- 0.08
t  <- 0:(length(cf) - 1)
NPV <- sum(cf / (1 + r)^t)
NPV

[1] 22614.27


A small investment with a positive NPV of about NT$22,300 — the project creates value.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
The IRR is the discount rate that makes \(NPV = 0\): \[\sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1+\text{IRR})^t} = 0.\]

npv <- function(r, cf) {
  t <- 0:(length(cf) - 1)
  sum(cf / (1 + r)^t)
}
irr <- uniroot(npv, interval = c(-0.99, 1), cf = cf)$root
irr

[1] 0.1709537


If IRR exceeds your required return, accept the project — equivalent to \(NPV > 0\) when cash flows are conventional.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
section: How much to save for retirement?
text:
How much to save for retirement?
You are 25, want NT$10,000,000 by age 65, earning 6% per year. How much do you need to save each year?
Rearrange the future-value-of-annuity formula:
\[FV = C \cdot \frac{(1+r)^n - 1}{r}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
C = \frac{FV \cdot r}{(1+r)^n - 1}\]

target <- 10000000; r <- 0.06; n <- 40
C <- target * r / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
C

[1] 64615.36


Only about NT$64,600 per year — the power of compounding over 40 years.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
What if you wait until 35?

target <- 10000000; r <- 0.06; n <- 30
C <- target * r / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
C

[1] 126489.1


NT$126,500 per year — nearly double, just by starting 10 years later.
Lesson: time is the most expensive variable in any financial plan.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
The monthly payment formula
A fully-amortizing loan of principal \(L\) at monthly rate \(r_m = r/12\) over \(N\) months has constant monthly payment:
\[M = L \cdot \frac{r_m \cdot (1+r_m)^N}{(1+r_m)^N - 1}\]
This is just the annuity-payment formula from earlier, applied monthly.

monthly_payment <- function(L, annual_rate, years) {
  r_m <- annual_rate / 12
  N   <- years * 12
  L * r_m * (1 + r_m)^N / ((1 + r_m)^N - 1)
}

For a 3-year grace period, the first 36 months are interest-only (monthly payment = \(L \cdot r_m\)), and the remaining principal then amortizes over 27 years — a second call to monthly_payment() with years = 27.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Comparing the six scenarios


Code
loans <- c(20e6, 15e6, 10e6)
rate  <- 0.022

# All six (loan × scheme) combinations
scenarios <- tibble(
  loan   = rep(loans, each = 2),
  scheme = rep(c("No grace", "3-yr grace"), times = 3)
) |>
  mutate(
    pmt_yr1to3 = if_else(scheme == "No grace",
                         monthly_payment(loan, rate, 30),
                         loan * rate / 12),                          # interest only
    pmt_yr4on  = if_else(scheme == "No grace",
                         monthly_payment(loan, rate, 30),
                         monthly_payment(loan, rate, 27)),           # amortize over 27 yr
    total_paid     = pmt_yr1to3 * 36 + pmt_yr4on * (30 * 12 - 36),
    total_interest = total_paid - loan
  )








The grace period lowers the first three years, but the post-grace payment is higher (the same principal must amortize in 27 years instead of 30) — and total interest paid is larger.

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
section: Where does the money actually go?
text:
Where does the money actually go?
Each monthly payment splits between interest and principal. In the early years almost all of it is interest — so the debt balance shrinks very slowly. The closed-form remaining balance after \(k\) months is \[B_k = L \cdot (1+r_m)^k - M \cdot \frac{(1+r_m)^k - 1}{r_m}\]

# Remaining balance after k months for a fully-amortizing loan
balance_amort <- function(L, annual_rate, years, k) {
  r_m <- annual_rate / 12
  M   <- monthly_payment(L, annual_rate, years)
  L * (1 + r_m)^k - M * ((1 + r_m)^k - 1) / r_m
}
# remaining after 24 years (24*12 months)
balance_amort(20e6, 0.025, 30, 24*12)

[1] 5278476

# remaining after 10 years
balance_amort(20e6, 0.025, 30, 10*12)

[1] 14912955

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
Visualizing the payment paths


Code
paths <- expand.grid(loan   = loans,
                     scheme = c("No grace", "3-yr grace"),
                     month  = 1:(30 * 12)) |>
  mutate(
    payment = case_when(
      scheme == "No grace"                 ~ monthly_payment(loan, rate, 30),
      scheme == "3-yr grace" & month <= 36 ~ loan * rate / 12,
      scheme == "3-yr grace" & month >  36 ~ monthly_payment(loan, rate, 27)
    ),
    loan_label = paste0("NT$", loan / 1e6, "M")
  )

# Compute the average monthly payment per (loan, scheme) over the full 30 years
payment_summary <- paths |>
  group_by(loan_label, scheme) |>
  summarise(avg_payment = mean(payment), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(payment_summary,
       aes(x = loan_label, y = avg_payment / 1000, fill = scheme)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(round(avg_payment / 1000))),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No grace"   = "#234E70",
                               "3-yr grace" = "#D9534F")) +
  labs(title = "Average monthly mortgage payment over 30 years",
       subtitle = "By loan size and grace-period scheme",
       x = "Loan size", y = "Average monthly payment (NT$ thousand)",
       fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Week 2: The Time Value of Money
text:
The takeaway
The grace period is not free money — it is a re-timing of cash flows. You pay less in years 1–3 and more in years 4–30, plus extra interest over the full life of the loan.
When does a grace period make sense?

You expect your income to rise significantly within a few years.
You face large one-time expenses early in the loan (renovation, kids).
You can invest the cash saved early at a higher rate than 2.2% — the same time-value-of-money logic in reverse.

When does it not?

You can already afford the level payment comfortably.
You want to minimize total interest paid over the life of the loan.

The Week 4 lesson on investment opportunity cost will sharpen this intuition further.

text:
Reading R’s error messages
R’s errors look intimidating but follow a pattern. The three you’ll meet most often:
1. Typo in a variable name
print(num_vra)
#> Error: object 'num_vra' not found
\(\Rightarrow\) Check spelling. R is case-sensitive: Apple \(\neq\) apple.
2. Forgotten quotes around a string
char_var <- Hello, R!
#> Error: unexpected ',' in "char_var <- Hello,"
\(\Rightarrow\) Strings need quotes: "Hello, R!".
3. Mismatched parentheses or braces
mean(c(1, 2, 3)
#> + 
\(\Rightarrow\) The + prompt means R is waiting for you to close a bracket. Press Esc and check.
Habit to build: when stuck, read the error from bottom to top. The last line usually says exactly what went wrong.

text:
The grammar of ggplot2
ggplot2 builds charts in layers, like sentences from grammar:

ggplot(data, aes(...)) — the subject: which data, and which columns map to which visual properties (x-axis, y-axis, color, size).
geom_line(), geom_point(), geom_bar()… — the verb: how to draw each row (a line? a dot? a bar?).
labs(), theme_*(), scale_*() — the adjectives: titles, themes, colors, axis formats.

You add layers with +. This is the only ggplot syntax you really need to remember:
ggplot(data, aes(x = ..., y = ...)) +
  geom_xxx() +
  labs(...) +
  theme_xxx()
Everything else is just looking up which geom_* you want.

title: Week 4: Portfolio Returns and Diversification
text:
You have NT$1,000,000 and want to invest it.
You could put it all in one stock. But two centuries of theory and practice say:
Spread it across many.
The reason is that combining imperfectly-correlated assets reduces the volatility of your wealth without reducing the expected return proportionally.
This is the central insight of modern portfolio theory (Markowitz, 1952).

You have NT$1,000,000 and want to invest it.
You could put it all in one stock. But two centuries of theory and practice say:

section: Portfolio return — two paths to the same number
text:
Portfolio return — two paths to the same number

Path A: from total portfolio value

portfolio <- portfolio |>
  mutate(R_disc = total_value / lag(total_value) - 1,
         r_log  = log(total_value / lag(total_value)))



Path B: weighted average of individual returns
\[R_p = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \, R_i\] The cross-section additivity result from Week 3.

title: Week 4: Portfolio Returns and Diversification
Week 4: Portfolio Returns and Diversification
text:
A single stock’s volatility
We measure risk by the standard deviation of its returns:
\[\sigma_i = \sqrt{\,\mathrm{Var}(R_i)\,}\]

vol_table <- indiv |>
  drop_na(R_disc) |>
  group_by(symbol) |>
  summarise(sigma = sd(R_disc))
vol_table

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  symbol  sigma
  <chr>   <dbl>
1 AAPL   0.0161
2 NVDA   0.0316
3 WMT    0.0125
4 XOM    0.0142


This is the total volatility of each stock.

title: Week 4: Portfolio Returns and Diversification
text:
Portfolio volatility — the key formula
For an \(N\)-asset portfolio with weights \(\mathbf{w}\) and a covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) of asset returns:






NotePortfolio variance and volatility



\[\sigma_p^{\,2} = \mathbf{w}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\, \mathbf{w},
\qquad
\sigma_p = \sqrt{\mathbf{w}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\, \mathbf{w}}.\]


The portfolio’s volatility is not the weighted average of the individual volatilities. The covariances matter.

title: Week 4: Portfolio Returns and Diversification
text:
The covariance matrix in R

returns_wide <- indiv |>
  drop_na(R_disc) |>
  select(symbol, date, R_disc) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = symbol, values_from = R_disc)

cov_matrix <- cov(returns_wide[ , -1], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
round(cov_matrix, 6)

          XOM      WMT     NVDA     AAPL
XOM  0.000203 0.000018 0.000000 0.000043
WMT  0.000018 0.000157 0.000023 0.000054
NVDA 0.000000 0.000023 0.001001 0.000191
AAPL 0.000043 0.000054 0.000191 0.000260


The diagonal is each stock’s variance. The off-diagonals are how the stocks move together.

title: Week 4: Portfolio Returns and Diversification
text:
Computing \(\sigma_p\) via matrix algebra

weights <- c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25)   # XOM WMT NVDA AAPL

port_var <- t(weights) %*% cov_matrix %*% weights
port_sd  <- sqrt(port_var)
port_sd

           [,1]
[1,] 0.01192684


%*% is matrix multiplication.
Compare port_sd against mean(vol_table$sigma) — the portfolio is less volatile than the average individual stock. That is diversification.

title: Week 4: Portfolio Returns and Diversification
text:
Why correlation matters
Decompose the variance formula for \(N = 2\):
\[\sigma_p^{\,2}
= w_1^2 \sigma_1^2 + w_2^2 \sigma_2^2
+ 2\, w_1 w_2\, \rho_{12}\, \sigma_1 \sigma_2.\]

\(\rho_{12} = +1\): no diversification, \(\sigma_p = w_1\sigma_1 + w_2\sigma_2\).
\(\rho_{12} = 0\): substantial reduction.
\(\rho_{12} = -1\): in principle, \(\sigma_p\) can be driven to zero.

Real stocks tend to have correlations of 0.3–0.8 with each other — enough for diversification to bite, but not enough to eliminate market risk.

title: Week 4: Portfolio Returns and Diversification
text:
The correlation matrix

cor_matrix <- cor(returns_wide[ , -1], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
round(cor_matrix, 2)

      XOM  WMT NVDA AAPL
XOM  1.00 0.10 0.00 0.19
WMT  0.10 1.00 0.06 0.27
NVDA 0.00 0.06 1.00 0.37
AAPL 0.19 0.27 0.37 1.00


Look at the off-diagonal entries: pairs with lower correlation contribute more to volatility reduction.

Equal-Weighted vs. 100% NVDA






A single-stock portfolio can crush a diversified one in a good year. It can also collapse spectacularly. Compare both return and volatility, not just return.

2.3. Simulate the MA Strategy

capital  <- 1000000
position <- 0
cash     <- capital
portfolio_ma <- data.frame()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(etf_ma_signals))) {
  date_i  <- etf_ma_signals$date[i]
  price_i <- etf_ma_signals$adjusted[i]
  sig     <- etf_ma_signals$signal[i]

  if (!is.na(sig)) {
    if (sig == "buy") {
      position_new <- floor(cash / price_i)
      position <- position + position_new
      cash     <- cash - position_new * price_i
    } else if (sig == "sell") {
      cash     <- cash + position * price_i
      position <- 0
    }
  }
  total_value <- cash + position * price_i
  portfolio_ma <- bind_rows(portfolio_ma,
                   data.frame(date = date_i, price = price_i,
                              position, cash, total_value))
}

final_ma  <- tail(portfolio_ma$total_value, 1)
return_ma <- (final_ma - capital) / capital * 100
cat("MA Strategy — Final Value: NT$", round(final_ma, 0),

title: R Note 4 - Trading Strategy
text:
3. RSI Strategy
The Relative Strength Index (RSI) measures the speed and change of recent price movements on a scale from 0 to 100. Unlike the MA crossover, which is a trend-following rule, RSI is a mean-reversion indicator: extreme readings suggest the asset is overbought or oversold and likely to reverse.
\[RSI = 100 - \frac{100}{1 + RS}, \quad RS = \frac{\text{Average Gain (14 days)}}{\text{Average Loss (14 days)}}\]
The standard thresholds are:

RSI < 30 → oversold → Buy
RSI > 70 → overbought → Sell


3.1. Compute RSI

etf_rsi <- etf_data |> 
  mutate(RSI = RSI(adjusted, n = 14))

4. Bollinger Bands Strategy
Bollinger Bands place an envelope around a moving average using the rolling standard deviation of prices. When prices hit the lower band, the market is considered locally cheap (buy); when prices hit the upper band, it is considered locally expensive (sell).
\[\text{Upper Band} = MA_{20} + 2\,\sigma_{20}, \qquad
\text{Lower Band} = MA_{20} - 2\,\sigma_{20}\]
where \(\sigma_{20}\) is the 20-day rolling standard deviation of the adjusted close.

4.1. Compute Bollinger Bands

bb <- BBands(etf_data$adjusted, n = 20, sd = 2)

etf_bb <- etf_data |> 
  mutate(
    BB_lower = bb[, "dn"],
    BB_mid   = bb[, "mavg"],
    BB_upper = bb[, "up"],
    pct_b    = bb[, "pctB"]   # percent-B: 0 = lower band, 1 = upper band
  )

5. Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA)
The three strategies above all require market-timing decisions. Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA) abandons timing entirely. Instead, the investor commits a fixed amount of money — say NT$30,000 — on the first trading day of each month, regardless of whether the market is up or down.
The key insight is that the same fixed amount buys more shares when prices are low and fewer shares when prices are high, automatically creating a form of anti-cyclical investing.

5.1. Simulate Monthly DCA
We set aside the full NT$1,000,000 as the cash reserve from day one and deploy NT$30,000 on the first trading day of each month. Any undeployed cash earns no return (a conservative assumption that ignores money-market interest).

monthly_invest <- 30000       # NT$ invested each month
total_reserve  <- 1000000     # cash reserve (never more than this deployed in total)

# Identify the first trading day of each month
first_trading_days <- etf_data |>
  mutate(ym = format(date, "%Y-%m")) |>
  group_by(ym) |>
  slice_min(date, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(date) |>
  pull()

# Simulate DCA
cash_dca      <- total_reserve
shares_dca    <- 0
portfolio_dca <- data.frame()
total_invested <- 0   # track cumulative cash deployed

for (i in seq_len(nrow(etf_data))) {
  date_i  <- etf_data$date[i]
  price_i <- etf_data$adjusted[i]

  # On the first trading day of each month, buy as many whole shares as possible
  # with the monthly budget (if cash is still available)
  if (date_i %in% first_trading_days && cash_dca >= monthly_invest) {
    new_shares  <- floor(monthly_invest / price_i)
    cost        <- new_shares * price_i
    shares_dca  <- shares_dca + new_shares
    cash_dca    <- cash_dca   - cost
    total_invested <- total_invested + cost
  }

  total_value <- cash_dca + shares_dca * price_i
  portfolio_dca <- bind_rows(portfolio_dca,
                    data.frame(date = date_i, price = price_i,
                               shares = shares_dca, cash = cash_dca,
                               total_value, total_invested))
}

final_dca  <- tail(portfolio_dca$total_value, 1)
deployed   <- tail(portfolio_dca$total_invested, 1)
return_dca <- (final_dca - capital) / capital * 100
cat("DCA Strategy — Final Value: NT$", round(final_dca, 0),
    "| Total Deployed: NT$", round(deployed, 0),
    "| Total Return:", round(return_dca, 2), "%\n")

Because the strategies start at slightly different points (MA requires 50 days of warm-up; RSI requires 14 days; BB requires 20 days), we align all series from the first date available in the MA strategy to ensure a common start.

text:
8. Discussion: What Does This Tell Us?

8.1. Timing strategies vs. passive accumulation
The three technical strategies (MA, RSI, Bollinger Bands) all require the investor to be out of the market for some stretches. That idle cash earns nothing in our simulation. DCA, by contrast, is always partially in the market — it accumulates shares steadily, month by month.


8.2. The DCA perspective
DCA is not designed to maximize returns during a bull market — it will lag a lump-sum buy-and-hold when prices trend up monotonically. Its strength lies in reducing the regret risk of investing a large lump sum at a market peak. Consider two scenarios:

Lump-sum investor who puts in NT$1M on January 2, 2023.
DCA investor who puts in NT$20,000 per month from the same date.

If prices fall mid-year, the DCA investor buys additional shares at the lower price, effectively lowering their average cost. The lump-sum investor is fully exposed from day one and cannot benefit from the dip.


8.3. Risk-adjusted performance
The Sharpe ratio is the classic tool for comparing strategies that carry different levels of volatility. A strategy with a lower raw return but much lower volatility can have a higher Sharpe ratio than a more volatile winner. Look at the summary table above for the full picture.


What we ignored
All simulations above share several unrealistic assumptions that a real investor must account for:

Transaction costs: brokerage commissions, securities transaction taxes (0.3% in Taiwan on sales), and market impact.
Slippage: we assume trades execute at the daily close price, which is never guaranteed.
Bid-ask spread: 0050.TW is highly liquid, but the spread still exists.
Opportunity cost of idle cash: in the MA and RSI strategies, cash held between signals earns nothing.

Introduction
In this document, we estimate factor models for a stock’s returns. A factor model decomposes a stock’s return into systematic components driven by common risk factors and a residual idiosyncratic component. We begin with the simplest case — the market model (one factor: the market return) — and progressively extend it to the Fama-French three-factor model (Fama and French, 1993) and the Carhart four-factor model (Carhart, 1996), which adds a momentum factor.
The general \(K\)-factor model is:
\[R_{i,t} - R_{f,t} = \alpha_i + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \beta_{i,k} \, F_{k,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t}\]
where \(R_{f,t}\) is the risk-free rate, \(F_{k,t}\) are factor returns (e.g., market, size, value, momentum), and \(\beta_{i,k}\) are the corresponding factor loadings estimated by OLS.

# Load required packages
library(tidyquant)
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(DT)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)
library(highcharter)
library(frenchdata)  # install.packages("frenchdata")

1. Fetching Stock Data
We collect daily adjusted price data for NVIDIA (NVDA) using tidyquant. The estimation window spans 2020–2022, a three-year horizon commonly used in empirical finance.1

stock_ticker  <- "NVDA"
market_ticker <- "^GSPC"

start_date <- "2020-01-01"
end_date   <- "2022-12-31"

stock_data  <- tq_get(stock_ticker,  from = start_date, to = end_date)
market_data <- tq_get(market_ticker, from = start_date, to = end_date)


Preview Data

datatable(stock_data) |> 
  formatRound(columns = c("open","high","low","close","adjusted"), digits = 2)

title: R Note 3 - Factor Model Estimation
R Note 3 - Factor Model Estimation
text:
3. The Market Model (One-Factor Model)
The market model is the simplest factor model. It regresses a stock’s excess return on the market excess return:2
\[R_{i,t} - R_{f,t} = \alpha_i + \beta_i \,(R_{m,t} - R_{f,t}) + \varepsilon_{i,t}\]
where:

\(\alpha_i\) is the stock’s abnormal return independent of the market.
\(\beta_i\) is the market beta — the sensitivity of the stock’s excess return to the market excess return. This is the measure of systematic risk.
\(\varepsilon_{i,t}\) is the idiosyncratic component unexplained by the market.


Scatterplot: NVDA vs. S&P 500


Code
fit_market <- lm(stock_return ~ market_return, data = returns_data)
returns_data$fit <- predict(fit_market)

highchart() |>
  hc_title(text = "Linear Relation: NVDA vs. S&P 500") |>
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = "Market Return (S&P 500)")) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Stock Return (NVDA)")) |>
  hc_add_series(data = returns_data,
                type = "scatter",
                hcaes(x = market_return, y = stock_return),
                name = "Daily Returns") |>
  hc_add_series(data = returns_data[order(returns_data$market_return), ],
                type = "line",
                hcaes(x = market_return, y = fit),
                name = "Fitted Line") |>
  hc_tooltip(pointFormat = "Market: {point.x:.4f}<br>Stock: {point.y:.4f}") |>
  hc_legend(align = "center", verticalAlign = "bottom") |>
  hc_add_theme(hc_theme_smpl())








Regression Output

model_1f <- lm(stock_return ~ market_return, data = returns_data)
summary(model_1f)


Call:
lm(formula = stock_return ~ market_return, data = returns_data)

Residuals:

-0.084558 -0.014089 -0.001877  0.013956  0.112267 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   0.0012297  0.0008435   1.458    0.145    
market_return 1.6562134  0.0526407  31.463   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.02319 on 754 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.5676,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.5671 
F-statistic: 989.9 on 1 and 754 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16




Extracting \(\hat{\beta}\) and Idiosyncratic Volatility

beta_hat <- tidy(model_1f) |> 
  filter(term == "market_return") |> 
  pull(estimate)

idio_vol <- sd(resid(model_1f))

cat("Estimated market beta for", stock_ticker, ":", round(beta_hat, 4), "\n")

Estimated market beta for NVDA : 1.6562 

cat("Idiosyncratic volatility (residual SD):",   round(idio_vol, 6), "\n")

Idiosyncratic volatility (residual SD): 0.023171 




Variance Decomposition
The market model implies a clean decomposition of total variance:
\[\underbrace{\sigma_i^2}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{\beta_i^2 \,\sigma_m^2}_{\text{systematic}} + \underbrace{\sigma_{\varepsilon,i}^2}_{\text{idiosyncratic}}\]

sigma_total <- sd(returns_data$stock_return)
sigma_mkt   <- sd(returns_data$market_return)
sys_part    <- beta_hat^2 * sigma_mkt^2
idio_part   <- idio_vol^2

tibble(
  Component     = c("Total variance", "Systematic", "Idiosyncratic"),
  Value         = c(sigma_total^2, sys_part, idio_part),
  Fraction      = c(1, sys_part / sigma_total^2, idio_part / sigma_total^2)
) |> 
  datatable() |> 
  formatRound(columns = c("Value", "Fraction"), digits = 6)

title: R Note 3 - Factor Model Estimation
text:
5. The Fama-French Three-Factor Model
Fama and French (1993) argue that the market alone cannot fully explain the cross-section of expected returns. Two additional factors capture systematic risks related to firm size and book-to-market ratio:
\[R_{i,t} - R_{f,t} = \alpha_i + \beta_i^{MKT}\,\text{MktRF}_t + \beta_i^{SMB}\,\text{SMB}_t + \beta_i^{HML}\,\text{HML}_t + \varepsilon_{i,t}\]

MktRF (Market Risk Premium): \(R_m - R_f\). The market factor; same as the CAPM.
SMB (Small Minus Big): average return of small-cap portfolios minus large-cap portfolios. Captures the size premium.
HML (High Minus Low): average return of high book-to-market (value) portfolios minus low book-to-market (growth) portfolios. Captures the value premium.


5.1 Merging Stock Returns with French Factors

# Restrict factors to the estimation window
ff3_est <- ff3_daily |> 
  filter(date >= start_date, date <= end_date)

# Compute stock excess return: stock_return - RF
ff3_merged <- returns_data |> 
  left_join(ff3_est |> select(date, MktRF, SMB, HML, RF), by = "date") |> 
  mutate(excess_return = stock_return - RF) |> 
  na.omit()

datatable(ff3_merged |> select(date, excess_return, MktRF, SMB, HML)) |> 
  formatRound(columns = c("excess_return","MktRF","SMB","HML"), digits = 5)







5.2 Regression: Fama-French Three-Factor Model

model_ff3 <- lm(excess_return ~ MktRF + SMB + HML, data = ff3_merged)
summary(model_ff3)

lm(formula = excess_return ~ MktRF + SMB + HML, data = ff3_merged)

(Intercept)  0.001331   0.000686   1.940   0.0528 .  
MktRF        1.616106   0.042881  37.688   <2e-16 ***
SMB          0.108461   0.086459   1.254   0.2101    
HML         -0.902552   0.050859 -17.746   <2e-16 ***
---
